A Therapeutic Intervention to Facilitate a Three Year Old Boy's Development

Catherine Weinmann

Catherine Weinmann

London
517 Magnolia
Piedmont
California
U.S.A.

Catherine Weinmann  

Introduction

Adam, the little boy whose treatment this paper records, was brought to a child therapy clinic because his mother was concerned by his slow speech development. At two years six months, he had only acquired a few words, and showed little interest in learning more. I embarked on his treatment with the expectation of coming to understand the conflict which impeded his acquisition of speech. However, as the treatment progressed I found myself concerned primarily with responding to the child's expectation that I would meet certain emotional needs. I began to see that some essential needs had not been met by his environment, and that it was this which stood in the way of his development proceeding normally.

A. Freud (1968) wrote, “Not only does every infant have definite needs stemming from his unformed and unstructured state, but these needs also change and vary with ongoing development. At every stage of his growth the child needs help from definite environmental attitudes and suffers harm if this help is not forthcoming”. She went on to warn of the need to distinguish diagnostically between disorders stemming from the frustration of developmental needs, “deficiency illnesses”, and the “neurotic and developmental disorders in which the child's ego plays the central pathogenic role”. She drew attention to the therapeutic problems such cases present, noting that analysis will only affect the “neurotic superstructure which does not cause, (but) merely overlays, the basic damage to the personality”. However, she did suggest that if the child is young and still close in time to the frustration of his needs, treatment may meet his needs.

D.W. Winnicott (1965) wrote more specifically of the techniques needed to help patients with this type of developmental deficiency. The analyst must provide an environment which will “facilitate the maturational process”. He compared the subtle adaption which the analyst makes to the changing needs of his patient to that of the mother and her infant.

Livia Di Cagno and Franco Ravetto: Le Malattie Chroniche e Mortali dell’ Infanzia. L'Angoscia di Morte. (“Childhood chronic and terminal illnesses: The dread of death”.) Rome: “Il Pensiero Scientifico”, 1980. 180 pp.

Gabriella Grauso

Gabriella Grauso

Gabriella Grauso  

This book is the result of ten years' work carried out in various special units of the paediatric department of the Turin Policlinic at the University of Turin. The team, directed by Professor Di Cagno, Professor Ravetto, and eight colleagues, is composed mainly of child psychiatrists and psychologists. The importance of their analytic orientation and of continuing individual and group supervisions is repeatedly stressed, and a fruitful collaboration with analysts both Italian and English is acknowledged as essential to their work.

As the authors say in their preface, the absolute protagonist of this book is the “dread of death”, which is almost concretely present in every individual who has to live with a chronic or terminal illness. It is this struggle within the self and the interplay between “external” physical pain and internal reality that they attempt to face.

The central theme of the book is the child in pain, and his fight against death. This, and the interplay of often massive, unbearable projections of agony between him, his parents and the people involved in his care, makes the book very moving. It is painful reading indeed, but at the same time a positive and helpful experience. It engenders the hope that a constant and serious study, not only of the traumatic implications of a child's hospitalisation but also of his object relations, can lead to a better understanding of the dynamics underlying the pathological process and to a lessening of the most acute anxieties.

The theoretical frame of reference is derived from the work of Freud and Melanie Klein, and their insights regarding the child's very primitive unconscious phantasies of annihilation and death. If, on an unconscious level, the child experiences death as the result of an aggressive act rather than as a natural biological event, it is understandable that illness should heighten his persecutory anxieties which will then be projected into his parents and family.

The second and third chapters illustrate the problems underlying the dynamics of the special units set up for the diagnosis and treatment of chronic and terminal diseases. The term “tecnico” (perhaps the Italian equivalent of the English “worker”) is introduced to give a new name—and possibly a new function—to the psychoanalytically orientated child psychiatrist or psychologist. Again the stress is laid not on his presence in the unit as the “expert”, but on the common psychological dimension of the whole team and of the unit itself. This is perhaps better illustrated in what the authors call the “psychological image” of these special units.

Maria Rhode

Maria Rhode

Maria Rhode  

This book is one of the series, The Developing Child, edited by Jerome Bruner, Michael Cole and Barbara Lloyd. As such it is addressed to workers

113

professionally concerned with children as well as to parents and the general reader. The dual nature of the book's intended audience is reflected in the two main sources the author has drawn on. Zick Rubin is a professor of social psychology whose work, he writes, has been concerned largely with, adult behaviour; but he is also the father of a son. Thus we are given the results of academic research on children's friendships—for instance, on what kinds of factors influence the way they interact in different sorts of playgroups; but we are also given careful observations the author made of his own little boy's behaviour, as well as his detailed notes on older children attending pre-school playgroups in California. Children's logs on friendship that were collected by a teacher, extracts from teenagers' diaries, responses to interview questions, relevant sections from works of fiction—all these are brought into the discussion.

The book covers a wider area. (Chapter headings in themselves are proof of this: Do friends matter? The earliest friendships; What is a friend; The skills of friendship; Being friends; Losing friends; Boys, girls and groups; Cross-age friendships; Environment and friendship.) The book is suffused with the conviction that friends do matter; more generally, that children matter, and that how we as adults behave towards them matters very much. Repeated attempts are made to draw practical conclusions for parents and teachers from the academic research that is discussed.

Unfortunately, no unity is achieved in this book between Professor Rubin's voice as a social psychologist and his voice as a father. The observations are invariably telling, vividly recorded and stimulating to further thought However, the author never confronts the question of the scientific status of observation, and the implicit underlying assumption seems to remain that in itself it has no such status. This is a facet of what appears to be a profound theoretical mistrust, and possibly misunderstanding, of the clinical viewpoint—a mistrust surprising in one whose own observations are so acute.

Mia Kellmer Pringle (Ed): A Fairer Future for Children. National Children's Bureau and The Macmillan Press Ltd.1980: Hardback £12.50, Paperback £4.95.

Mary Boston

Mary Boston

Mary Boston  

This is a challenging book and one calculated to make us think about all our assumptions, implicit as well as explicit, not only about the needs of children but also our whole way of life.

Dr. Mia Kellmer Pringle, who is well known for her work as Director of the National Children's Bureau and for the wealth of research which she has initiated, not only reviews for us succinctly and comprehensively the latest research on the needs of the developing child but confronts us with the need to act on it in our social policies and economic arrangements.

She does not shirk from tackling courageously many controversial issues, such as sex differences, the effect of working mothers on the development of children, the adequacy of group day care for under threes. She puts forward powerful arguments, both logical and economic for making “prevention” a cornerstone of social policy.

She means prevention of emotional and intellectual neglect and deprivation as well as handicap in childhood. She advocates a long-term comprehensive policy for children “based on improving the quality of parenting, of health care and of education from cradle to adulthood”. The achievement of such a policy requires, in her view, “three wide ranging changes: first a different attitude to parenthood and child rearing; second, a willingness to provide more adequate supportive services for families and children; and third the acceptance both of children's rights to consistent, continuing, dependable, loving care and of parents' obligations to provide it”.

Dr. Kellmer Pringle suggests a radical change in our attitude to parenthood. She challenges the view that equality for women means “sameness” and criticises the current social pressures on women both to marry and have children and to “ape the male model” by competing in the world of paid employment, thus ending up overburdened by two jobs and unable to enjoy the children. She suggests that recognition should be given to the fact that bringing up children is one of the most skilled, fulfilling and responsible jobs, only to be undertaken by those with a vocation for it. Parenthood should be by choice, for those prepared to devote time to it. There could be a variety of patterns of parenting (and marriage) to allow for continuity of loving care for the children and to obviate the need for day care for under threes at least,—or preferably under fives.

When There were Monsters … Asthma, Anxiety, and Health in a Three-Year-Old Boy

Ellen Bitz

Ellen Bitz

65 Victoria Street
North Woodstock
Ontario, Canada

Ellen Bitz  

Introduction

Philip was referred to the Child and Family Psychiatric Clinic when he was three-and-a-half. In this paper I will concentrate on three important patterns to do with Philip's state of being at the time of referral:

Extreme sensitivity to inner and outer sensations linked to a feeling of extreme vulnerability and fragility and a need for things to be “just right”. This vulnerability, in time was heightened by a feeling of persecution from his own desire to break and spoil.

Entanglement with his mother and all his objects, which often took the form of sticking onto (like glue) or sticking into (like pins).

Use of words (symbols) in a precocious yet concrete way, making words into protective devices and into a private language.

I will argue that these three are all related to his underlying anxiety and go deeper than his three year old oedipal fears and feelings (e.g. comparing his penis — which he called a ‘spout’ — to his father's and to his younger brother's). He did have a particular reason to be anxious about his penis however, as he had undescended testicles and knew he would at some time have to have an operation to correct this.

I will try to show how therapy enabled him to feel safe and take the risks involved in growing up, without resorting to these defensive manoeuvres. It is important to note that these patterns, which may also be seen in autistic or psychotic children, were able to be touched and changed, and growth towards health to occur.

I will discuss how this was achieved partly by Philip's ability to regress to infantile feelings and behaviour (as if he “knew” what he needed) and then use his appropriate intelligence and imagination to integrate the regression. Here his use of words was helpful and not pathological. There was a strong impulse toward love, trust and growth in him and his family, and one of the joys of therapy and later follow-up was watching this impetus grow and develop.

I will use clinical material, especially from early and final sessions, to illustrate the discussion.

The following clinical report is based on a short-term, conjoint treatment of a 212 to 3 year old boy and his mother. First we will summarise observations gathered during an assessment period at the beginning of treatment. We will discuss our understanding of the developmental significance of this observational material and describe the set of clinical hypotheses which grew out of this understanding and guided the subsequent therapeutic work. The clinical case report proper will illustrate the application of the above issues to the treatment situation and be followed by a discussion of treatment outcomes and our understanding of the causes behind them.

Assessment Period

Six months before referral, when Andy was just two, there had been a terrible argument between Mr. and Mrs. Clayton, which took place outside Andy's bedroom. From his crib, Andy could only hear the angry, frightening words, and his father hitting his mother. His father left after the argument and was not seen again. Mr. and Mrs. Clayton were divorced soon afterwards. Mrs. Clayton became severely depressed and gave Andy no explanation of his father's disappearance. There had also not been any words on previous occasions to explain father's violent episodes which had punctuated family life, or his long absence when Andy was 3 to 15 months old. Mr. Clayton had a history of instability, including several short-term psychiatric hospitalisations.

When Andy was 212 years, Mrs. Clayton called the Child Development Project at the recommendation of Andy's nursery school. The referral came 2 weeks after he had entered full-time nursery school. Mrs. Clayton reported that the school staff was concerned about his incomprehensible speech, his lack of awareness of danger, his refusal to follow instructions, and his aggression toward other children. Mrs. Clayton wondered if these symptoms meant that Andy had inherited his father's mental illness.

The assessment included a school visit, 4 home visits, and a developmental testing (Stanford-Binet, L-M Form) session. At school, Andy's first week was difficult. Separations from mother at the beginning of the day were reported to be stressful. Andy cried at leave-taking and for a considerable period afterwards.

Rolene Szur  

These papers were originally presented at a scientific meeting of the Association of Child Psychotherapists, which included contributions from Dr. N. Lisman and Mrs. A. Fletcher.

It bas been said that Psycho-analysis discovered the child within the adult, and that child-analysis discovered the baby within the child. With the psychoanalytic study of Infant Observation the wheel began to turn full circle as the “little adult” within the baby came more clearly into view.*

This awareness of the continuities in the meaning of relationships from the beginning of life forms the basis of some work which has been carried out by a number of psychoanalysts and child psychotherapists in Infant Intensive Care Units and other wards. Although they have focussed in turn on the parents, on the babies, the staff, and the ward atmosphere as a whole, observations of mothers and babies have formed the core and common starting point.

In this context it is interesting to note that the last two decades or so have seen considerable developments within the fields of medicine and experimental psychology, which have become more subtle, as well as more sophisticated, in their studies of infant behaviour. A major common theme which has emerged might be summed up by a quotation from Newson, writing in 1977, that in contrast to their physical immaturity, infants are “in a sense highly precocious socially”. There is now “hard evidence” that from the very beginning, babies take an interest in people before objects, interacting and communicating in a social way, and that their senses enable them to distinguish mother's smell, voice, and face within the first days and weeks. This is welcome confirmation for the kind of findings which have been made by the more specifically psycho-analytic techniques of combining attentiveness to detail and sequence with receptivity and empathy, in order to follow the patterns of meaning and relationships which can be seen to emerge.

Working inside a ward in a hospital one encounters an interplay of medical emotional and personality factors.

The Baby: Action Consultancy

Averil Earnshaw

Averil Earnshaw

30 Straffan Lodge
1 Belsize Grove
London NW3

Averil Earnshaw  

Some time ago I began visiting a Special Care Baby Unit in a big hospital and observing there for one hour each week.

I had wanted to observe new prematurely born babies because I am interested in our very early responses to our environment, particularly in physical responses; this physical way is our only way of expressing ourselves before language develops and before there is much of a “memory bank” of experiences in this world. (Bick 1966)

Most of our early physical responses are reflex movements and automatic activities, and I wonder if very early patterns correlate with symptoms of illness in later life. In so many of the symptoms of psychosomatic illnesses there is an imbalance of autonomie control. In new-born babies I thought I would best be able to observe automatic reflex activity before more integrated purposeful movements developed.

Once I began visiting the unit, I realised that I was being observed by the staff there, and it was strange for them to find someone apparently doing nothing; I was taken for a grannie, an aunt, a midwife, a mum, and “one of those mad psychiatrists”. Gradually I was accepted as harmless, although odd, and nurses and parents began to talk to me. Nurses would often make thoughtful remarks about the babies, like “he must feel so exposed in this big incubator, after being inside”. I found myself observing the babies with my face almost touching the transparent side of the incubators, naturally finding an eight-inch space between us; I read that this has been shown to be the distance at which babies focus best,—and of course it is the distance between faces of mother and feeding baby.

As the weeks and months went by I felt more comfortable in the unit but increasingly uncomfortable at what I saw happening when the babies' temperatures were taken rectally. This was done 4 hourly and was always followed, when the thermometer was pushed in, by marked changes in the babies' respiration, general movement, facial expression and often colour. The changes are most marked in the newest and smallest babies. Respiration diminishes, sometimes to gasping or hiccoughing, while the thermometer is in the rectum, and when it is removed, over-ventilation very soon follows and persists. General movement usually slows, sometimes to the point of apparent collapse and flaccidity, when the thermometer is pushed in, but soon returns to normal. The facial expression alters drastically and the baby looks quite vacant. The investigatory procedures themselves seemed to be altering the babies' physiology.

Psychoanalysis and Serendipity: Their Place in Family Therapy

Gillian Parker

Gillian Parker

The Lincoln Tower
77 Westminster Bridge Road
London SEI 7HS.

Gillian Parker  

Introduction

The notions in this paper stem from my practice of working with “children-within-families', combining two approaches, that of the psycho-analyst interested in the unconscious phantasy of the individual, and the family therapist, who sees that distress never occurs in isolation, and is therefore interested in the group process and the language of the family myth.

Ferreira in 1965 pointed out that family myths can be seen as patterns of mutually agreed but distorted roles providing models and plans for social action. If a family has to use too many, or the roles played are too extreme, then the family acts in a very rigid way and the individuals are tied into a crippling performance. Byng-Hall (1973) shows that family myths of this kind originate within an unresolved crisis such as a failed mourning. He describes various ways in which the young may be recruited into the drama of the parents' inner world. Under the description of closed-circuit families I sought to show how very disturbed individuals share unconscious phantasies as a way of surviving (Elles 1961). Over decades and even generations, these family myths may be maintained without testing their “reality”. Thus they create a pathological focus of tension in the family member who must suffer a widening rift between privately held views and actions and family ordained experience. This is felt as the passively endured intrusions described by Heimann (1965).

Up to this point the myth can be seen only in pathological terms. Yet I would suggest that the myth can also stand for the seed of the family's actual past experience, and can be the important bridge between what at one point in time was unknowable and at another unknown.

The Family Myth as a Pathological Phenomenon

To illustrate these two points of view I have selected three cases of family myths encountered during analytic work with children in sick families and have compared these with depth interviews with some 20 “well” couples all expecting their first baby.

The Mother: Talking about the Birth

Judith Elkan

Judith Elkan

31 Coleridge Walk
London NW11

Judith Elkan  

In my observations on a maternity ward and in a paediatric unit I have been struck by the urgent desire demonstrated by mothers to recount the birth experience. I found that whether the birth had been easy or difficult, the mothers were glad to talk to someone who was interested, and to communicate details about the birth. It became clear to me that in telling their story these mothers were seeking an opportunity for recognition and acknowledgement of their emotions, and especially of the uniqueness of their own experience.

The object of this brief communication is to focus on the critical experience of labour and the events surrounding the birth, and to consider the effect on the mother of the ways these events are responded to. I shall give some illustrations of my own and a colleague and reflect on factors which may interfere with the capacity of staff to acknowledge emotions about the birth. I shall also discuss some implications for maternity care.

In the early days after the birth it is possible to observe that doubts and anxieties which a mother may harbour about her labour and the events surrounding it often encroach on her ease of mind and ability to attend to the newborn. In a traumatic birth the opportunity to communicate about the event can be of significance in dealing with these anxieties, thus freeing the mother to attend with greater ease to the care of the baby. My first example of a birth where the baby's life was seriously at risk illustrates the helpful role played by the birth attendant. The labour was fraught with difficulty, but in the event the baby survived and subsequently both parents took part in caring closely for the baby. Later on, the mother described how important for her and her husband had been the readiness of a staff member to come on the following day and talk about the birth. The midwife had spoken about the dangerous situation in labour. She said that at one stage she had thought the baby did not stand much chance of surviving and that she had just prayed. The parents, who had experienced acute anxiety during the labour, were extremely moved and very grateful to the midwife for coming to speak about the event. Her description helped to validate their own feelings about the life and death crisis their baby had gone through. They were then able to ask for more detail and, by understanding better the cause of the crisis, were also relieved of unnecessary guilt and anger about possible failures on the part of themselves or the hospital.

W. Freud  

I think it should be borne in mind that the following observations, made in various Neonatal Intensive Care Units (NICUs) in this country and in the United States, have taken place at a time when the medical profession realizes that in many respects the technology which made such spectacular advances and often left psychological considerations far behind seems to have reached its limits, so that there is time to pause and take stock. Concurrently, powerful social forces are questioning the authority of the hospital over its patient population. Moreover, competition for who “owns” the patient is gradually being replaced by considerations of how hospital and family can best complement each other to help the patient to help himself.

There is no doubt that the current hospital setting is still inhibiting and discourages mothers from having close physical contact with their babies. As one mother put it, when talking about her newborn: “When I get home I'll put him on the floor and I'll get to know him at last”.

Both hospital staff and mother (for short, I use “mother”, as she is the main caregiver) manifestly have the same aims: 1. that while the baby is in neonatal intensive care the mother should be helped to become confident in looking after him herself, and 2. that mother and infant should thrive so that they can be at home together as soon as possible. In fact, however, we often encounter somewhat puzzling manifestations that do not bear out this identity of interests. They begin to make sense only if we acknowledge the double-edged nature of the conscious and unconscious functioning in both staff and parents.

On a surface level we can discern the rational well-meaning intentions of hospital staff, but underneath staff have to distance themselves to cope with anxieties and conflicts over possessiveness and loss of authority. Similarly, mothers are manifestly motivated to be in frequent close physical touch with their infants, especially after having been separated from an at-risk baby after delivery. On a deeper level, however, they do not want to be reminded of their feelings of guilt, failure and incompetence and try as best they can to distance themselves. One can often identify various coping mechanisms which are used, like denial, avoidance, postponement and displacement. Mother and staff may often unconsciously collude in the use of such distancing devices. The collusions are reflected in various compromises that make good sense neither medically nor psychologically even though they are tolerated and perpetuated by staff and parents alike. Such apparent contradictions are more easily spotted by an outside observer.

Involvement with the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit arose out of a tradition of good liaison between the Department of Paediatrics and that of Child Psychiatry. Some five years ago requests were received to see parents of babies on the Unit.

Impact of Divorce on Children: Vicissitudes and Therapeutic Implications of the Reconciliation Fantasy

Rebecca Lohr MSW , Morton Chethik MSW , Steven Press MSW , Antal Solyom MD PHD and Ann Arbor

Ann Arbor

Michigan 48109
U.S.A.

Ann Arbor  

In our work with children of divorce, we have noted that the relinquishing of the parental unit as it serves the child's environmental and internal needs is a highly complex and painful process. Parental objects serve important internal, as well as external functions, and the loss of continuity in the parental relationship can serve as a “developmental interference”. After a divorce has occurred, a child may continue to have a relationship with both the custodial and non-custodial parent; however, there is inevitably a loss of the parental unit and the internal functions served by the child's relationship with that unit.

Children experience this loss in multi-determined ways, and attempt to handle it with the utilization of a variety of internal mechanisms. We have observed a striking and persistent fantasy in a number of children whose parents have divorced—the fantasy that the parents will be reconciled with one another and the lost family will be regained in some form. This paper will define the reconciliation fantasy, explore some of the determinants of its emergence and persistence in children of divorce, and discuss implications for therapeutic interventions.

Distinction between Reunion Wishes and Reconciliation Fantasies

The literature reflects no clear distinction between reunion wishes and reconciliation fantasies. Children who have been bereaved by the death of a parent have been cited as experiencing fantasies of being reunited with the lost parent (Nagera, 1970; Rochlin, 1953; Tessman, 1978; Wolfenstein, 1965).

Children of divorced parents have been noted to experience similar fantasies and wishes (Wallerstein and Kelly, 1976; Tessman, 1978). Reunion wishes in these instances imply the re-evoking of the lost object—through identification, acting out, or fantasies—and the continuation of the self's relationship with the object. The reconciliation fantasy, while it may take on certain aspects of the reunion wish, is used here to denote the child's wish for a continuation of the parental ties to one another as well as to the self. It may represent the wish, not for a return to the perhaps chaotic pre-separation state, but for an idealized reinstatement of the previous relationship.

Introduction

In this report I shall portray three crucial years of Steven's development, from the time of his father's death — just prior to Steven's third birthday — till the beginnings of latency at age six. I shall focus on tracing how aspects of the father's illness, death and the subsequent fatherless years affected Steven's development. He was helped by his mother with whom I worked throughout this period in a weekly treatment-via-the-parent and by the teaching staff of the Hanna Perkins Therapeutic Nursery School and Kindergarten where Steven had attended since he was three and a half years old (R.A. Furman and A. Katan, 1969). The therapeutic work was based on the mother's and teachers' observations, augmented by my own weekly visits at the school.

Although we kept open the option of individual analysis for Steven, during this period of work we considered treatment-via-the-parent to be the treatment of choice for several reasons: in spite of phase-appropriate difficulties, some neurotic manifestations, and a tendency to instinctual regression under stress, Steven maintained a progressive development. His defences had not calcified to the point of rigidity, nor had they been inadequate to binding his anxieties. Thus no serious inner obstacles interfered with access to his psychic life. The mother-child relationship was characterised by age-appropriate closeness and empathic mutual understanding as well as a shared knowledge of the past. Even at the height of distress at the beginning of our work, the mother functioned well in her parental role, was familiar with emotional development and its handling and keen on actively helping her boy. Aware of some of her weaknesses, she struggled valiantly to overcome them and largely succeeded. Apart from these more usual indications for treatment-via-the-parent, it seemed particularly important that, following the loss of the father, the mother-child relationship should not be interfered with by the introduction of an outsider — which the analyst inevitably is — unless it proved absolutely necessary.

Introduction

This paper describes the intensive psychotherapy of a severely disturbed boy. The child had a cleft palate and lip. The events surrounding the child's development illustrate a child unable to engage human beings as sources of comfort and well-being. The meaning for his life was obtained from the world of diesel trucks. Significant alterations in therapeutic interventions had to be implemented in order to engage the child in a meaningful relationship. During the course of therapy, the child progressed from being a “wild diesel” to a “diesel mechanic” and finally, to an “executive” of a “diesel company”. Therapy was successful in advancing the child from his pathological identification with diesels to more realistic identification with the therapist

The literature on the psychological implications for children of hospitalisation and surgery describes fears of abandonment, punishment, mutilation, disfigurement and pre-occupation with fantasies of violence and death (Becker, 1972; Bergman & Freud, 1965; Conway, 1975; Erikson, 1972; Jessner, Blom & Waldfogel, 1952). Children with cleft palate and lip experience surgery in their first year of life with follow-up surgery as they develop (Grabb, Rosenstein & Bzoch, 1971; Holdsworth, 1970). Some studies of these children focus primarily on assisting the parents in their attitudes, anxieties and misconceptions through a team approach of medical, dental and speech specialists (Baker, 1955; Lillywhite, 1956; Lowe, 1961; Subtelny, 1955). Tisza et al (1958) comment upon the extreme distortion of the mouth in figure drawings by cleft palate and lip children reflecting their body image perception. Alpert (1959) describes a boy with cleft palate being fixated at the oral stage with a compulsion to repeat injury to his mouth. Irwin and McWilliams (1974) report that the fantasies of these children depict themes of oral aggression, fears of bodily injury and fears of being attacked or killed. Tisza et al (1969) subjected the latter study to psychoanalytic interpretation concluding that the fantasies revealed fixation at the oral incorporative, oral, sadistic and phallic stages.

Christopher Reeves  

Some years ago Heimann drew attention to the comparative neglect of the anal stage in recent developments of psychoanalytic theory. In “Notes on the Anal Stage” (Heimann, 1962) she expressed the view that over-exclusive preoccupation with the oral stage has led to a distorted picture of childhood developmental processes, by portraying mechanisms as operating from birth which actually became established through gradual maturation. She saw a need to reappraise traditional concepts about the anal stage as a step towards remedying this imbalance.

Her principal contention was that in psychic processes of the anal stage lay the prototypes of all subsequent creative activities. Since the body functions are not directed towards other persons, “the fantasies involved in the anal sensations must be thought of as intrinsically devoid of object notions, fully narcissistic and incommunicable”. She criticised the tendency only to see in childhood anal behaviour fantasied sadistic attacks on the parents or their images. She also questioned the belief that the child was always prone in omnipotent fashion to overvalue his fashion products. That such thoughts and feelings might become associated with the child's excretory functions was not denied; but she disputed whether they were the primary motives for the child's acts of withholding or soiling. Instead of these conventional and rather condemnatory appraisals, Heimann suggested that strivings for anal mastery reveal the first signs of the child's emerging ego-autonomy allied to a benign narcissism necessary for healthy creativity. Hence the importance of this stage, not only for the child, but also for our understanding of many ego functions.

Mention of terms like “ego-autonomy”, “creativity” and “benign forms of narcissism” might lead one to suppose that Heimann's fresh ideas about the anal stage had fallen on fertile soil. Several major additions to psycho-analytic literature in recent years (e.g. Winnicott, 1971; Milner, 1969; Kohut, 1971) witness to the attention nowadays being paid to the links between ego-development, integration, and healthy investment of the self-image on the one hand, and satisfaction in object-relationships and later creative endeavours on the other. One thinks particularly of Winnicott's exhaustive study of “transitional phenomena” arid their bearing on the development of the “unit-self, on play and the range of artistic and cultural expression.

Remarks on Aggression

Edith Buxbaum

Edith Buxbaum

6036 Upland Ter. S.
Seattle
WA98112

Edith Buxbaum  

At a meeting of the Sigmund Freud Institute, Frankfurt, in 1964, on a topic of “Aggression and Adaptation”, which to some degree was a discussion of Konrad Lorenz's just published book (1963), “Natural History of Aggression, the so-called Evil”, Paula Heimann participated and emphasised in her discussion the role of internalization which leads to a new kind of consciousness and being that sets men apart from animals. She wondered whether the appearance of cruelty could be considered a new form of aggression different from animal aggressivity that seems to be free of cruelty and only directed towards preservation of the species. It seems to me that the idea to separate cruelty from aggression in general is a new and interesting idea. It makes it possible to differentiate the destructive form of aggressivity derived from the death instinct from the constructive form which Freud originally called self-preservation and which agrees with the Darwinian idea of evolution and the survival of the fittest Spitz, in his paper ‘To the Adaptation Promoting Role of Aggression’ (1968), says that “without aggression, without the forces and tools drawn from it, there would be no evolution”.* Aggression is not only destructive, it is the life instinct, it-is life itself. Without it nothing would work, we would not work. Energy in itself is neither good nor evil, but can be used either way. So it is with aggression. It is at least as adaptable as the sexual drive, if not more so. When the sex drive is frustrated, it may change to anger, hatred, revenge—by mobilizing the aggressive drive, which is admixed with it. For sex itself needs a certain amount of aggression to set itself in motion. Aggression is not only destructive. Freud himself did not see it that way for a long time. He looked upon it as “ego-instinct” and identified it with the self-preservative instinct in contrast to libido. Only in 1930 in the VIth Chapter of “Civilization and its Discontents” did he give special consideration to the aggressive and destructive instincts for the first time. He had earlier paid little attention to these except where they were fused with libidinal elements, but he now discussed them in their pure form and explained them as derivatives of the death instinct†. In the “New Introductory Lectures” (1933) Freud says: “Our hypothesis is that there are two essentially different classes of instincts: the sexual instincts, understood in the widest sense—Eros, if you prefer that name—and the aggressive instincts, whose aim is destruction”.

A Modern Pilgrim's Progress: Reminiscences of Personal Analysis with Dr. Bion

Frances Tustin

Frances Tustin

17 Orchard Lane
Amersham
Buckinghamshire

Frances Tustin  

Some years ago Dr. Bion suggested that I might write a book for the general reader about my personal experience of psycho-analysis. I am not yet ready to do that but, when the Editor of this Journal approached me to write a short article about the experience of analysis with Dr. Bion, I remembered the title I had thought of for such a book—“A Modem Pilgrim's Progress”. Inevitably, this title arises from the religious background in which I was reared. Although I value this, I now conceive of it in somewhat different terms. For the modem pilgrim, the final goal is not the Heaven which Bunyan envisaged, but a step into the unknown which Bion so eloquently and disturbingly placed before us. The purpose of this article is to try to give fellow travellers a brief glimpse of the pilgrimage I embarked upon under his auspices which led into dark comers of the mind I never realised existed.

I have often been asked whether Dr. Bion talked in the somewhat inscrutable, oracular way in which he sometimes wrote. I can say very firmly that this was not so. He was always brief, to the point and extremely simple and clear. Those who attended those memorable meetings in the Tavistock Clinic where he discussed with the audience any topic which arose will know what I mean about his simplicity and clarity. But he was very disturbing. The muted, complacent, safe reactions by which I had managed my life until I met him were upsettingly disturbed. I remember clearly the first time I met Dr. Bion to arrange the times of our analytic meetings. I thought I had never met anyone I disliked quite so much. As well as indicating my own intransigent resistance to analysis, I think it indicates the strong feelings which Dr. Bion aroused. He was not the sort of person towards whom one could have a halfhearted reaction. However, during the first week I had quite different thoughts from the ones I had had at that first meeting. With a sense of awe I thought, “I've got something rare here”. (Both Dr. Bions were “awful” or perhaps I should say “awesome”).

A Commemorative Essay on W.R. Bion's Theory of Thinking

Edna O'Shaughnessy

Edna O'Shaughnessy

20 Heath Drive
London NW3

Edna O'Shaughnessy  

When W.R. Bion died in 1979 his own work, in his lifetime, had changed psycho-analysis. He made clinical discoveries which led him to formulate new concepts and original theories over a wide spectrum of fundamental psychoanalytic problems. Because of its close connection to new ways of working with patients, I have chosen as the topic of this commemorative essay Bion's work on thinking.

Bion formulated a theory of the origins of thinking. He posited an early first form of thinking, different from but the basis for the development of, later forms. This first form of thinking strives to know psychic qualities, and is the outcome of early emotional events between a mother and her infant which are decisive for the establishment—or not—of the capacity to think in the infant. Bion's theory, which carries the interesting implication that knowledge of the psychological precedes knowledge of the physical world, represents a new understanding of thinking as one of the fundamental links between human beings, a link which is fundamental also for the forming and functioning of a normal mind. Throughout Bion connected his work on thinking to analytic technique and so made possible clinical advances with patients of all ages.

It is not easy to convey the rare originality of Bion's thought. He expressed himself in austere propositions with a high yield of exact meaning. They repay the reader's repeated return, as, for diversion, do his occasional and lastingly funny jokes. My plan is first to summarize some of the main aspects of his work on thinking and then give clinical illustrations of its use in child analysis.

What does Bion mean by ‘thinking’? He does not mean some abstract mental process. His concern is with thinking as a human link—the endeavour to understand, comprehend the reality of, get insight into the nature of, etc., oneself or another. Thinking is an emotional experience of trying to know oneself or someone else. Bion designates this fundamental type of thinking—thinking in the sense of trying to know — by the symbol K. If xKy, then “x is in the state of getting to know y and y is in a state of getting to be known by x”.

Lore Schact

Lore Schact

Freiburg
Höchte Strasse 38
7831 Sexan
West Germany

Lore Schact  

The world as experience belongs to the basic world I-It. The basic word I-You establishes the world of relation.

Relation is reciprocity… inscrutably involved, we live in the currents of universal reciprocity.

Martin Buber

In his paper “Mirror-role of Mother and Family in Child Development” (1967), D.W. Winnicott assigns a special significance to the mirroring function of the mother's face in the development of the child's self. He bases his ideas on the observation of the infant-mother-relationship as well as on reconstructions from his experience with adult patients who had regressed to the dependence of infancy.

“What does the baby see when he or she looks at the mother's face? I am suggesting that, ordinarily, what the baby sees is himself or herself. In other words the mother is looking at the baby and what she looks like is related to what she sees there. All this is too easily taken for granted. I am asking that this which is naturally ‘done well by mothers who are caring for their babies shall not be taken for granted. I can make my point by going straight over to the case of the baby whose mother reflects her own mood or, worse still, the rigidity of her own defences. In such a case what does the baby see? Of course nothing can be said about the single occasions on which a mother could not respond. Many babies, however, do have to have a long experience of not getting back what they are giving. They look and they do not see themselves. There are consequences. Firstly, their own creative capacity begins to atrophy, and in some way or other they look around for other ways of getting something of themselves back from the environment”.

In the same paper, Winnicott (1967) describes what happens when the mother's face does not function as a mirror with its extreme consequences of an experience of menacing chaos by the baby. The baby may then react by withdrawal into itself or it may just look at the world in order to perceive.

“A baby so treated will grow up puzzled about mirrors and what the mirror has to offer. If the mother's face is unresponsive, then a mirror is a thing to be looked at but not to be looked into”.

Judith Trowell

Judith Trowell

120 Belsize Lane
London NW3 5BA.

Judith Trowell  

Introduction

This is an attempt to understand overwhelming psychotic material and mad behaviour in a child seen for therapy at four years of age. Very often I wondered if this child was so disturbed that she needed special placement; was I continuing therapy where I should be suggesting alternative arrangements such as a total therapeutic environment? How could I expect this child to cope in a normal school and to continue living at home? In the beginning I took her into therapy because she said ‘I'm frightened” during my first interview. Despite the psychotic behaviour and the intense psychotic transference, there continued to be moments of contact between us although few and far between. I think this gave me the courage to continue in the belief that beneath the maelstrom there was a person, not a psychotic emptiness. Perhaps a child behaving in this way should sometimes be seen as reacting constructively, not as mounting an assault on functioning but hoping someone can survive the attacks and understand.

During therapy there were three moments when change clearly occurred; these were all prior to breaks in the treatment The breaks can be seen as a relief, confirmation for her that she was not mixed up with the object but separate, we were not muddled together. The therapy allowed the child to internalise the whole therapist good and bad, with strengths and weaknesses she had fully explored. The internalised Dr. Trowell could contain and accept all of herself so that she herself could begin to understand. She did not then need to expend all her energy in maintaining a defensive barrage, in attacking and destroying the me in her memory and mind. Unlike a psychotic child she appeared able to use the internalised me in a positive way, to hold her over the breaks and enable her to continue to work. This then is an account of a very disturbed child who benefited from twice a week therapy.

Anna was presented as a child who ate reluctantly and who had difficulties in making relationships. In a preliminary interview she had made an intricate plasticene model of an ideal garden and had appeared as a self contained, precociously adult child with a fragile, disturbed mother. Before reviewing the therapy with Anna, I shall describe my first encounter with her to try and share the impact this child had on me from the start.

Frances Tustin: Autistic States in Children, Published by Routledge and Kegan Paul Ltd.1981 Price £12.50.

Anne Alvarez

Anne Alvarez

Anne Alvarez  

This eloquent book concerns itself with the diagnosis, theory and psychotherapy of autistic states in childhood. Although the author's acquaintance with the psychiatric and psychoanalytic literature on autism and childhood schizophrenia is vast, her understanding of the various diagnostic and theoretical problems is always communicated in simple but powerful language which even the lay reader may grasp. In a chapter entitled, “Psychological Birth and Psychological Catastrophe”, she concludes with the following statement:

“The therapeutic setting acts as a kind of incubator in which the psychological “prem” can achieve those basic integrations he did not make in infancy. These extreme states are usually worked over within the privacy of parental sheltering. It seems somewhat indecent to lay them bare. Perhaps this is one of the reasons why psychosis seems so shocking and disturbing to normal individuals. Something is made public which should be kept private. Analysing such states seems rather like trying to put a dream or nightmare under a microscope. It just cannot be done. It is a paradox that these crude states need extreme delicacy and subtlety in their delineation. To write about them often seems brash and clumsy, but not to do so seems a professional derelication”.

The quotation may serve as a reminder of the enormous difficulty any writer in this field must face in trying to communicate his understanding of these children. What is extraordinary about Tustin's writing is that although it is metaphorical and evocative, (as she has suggested in her earlier book on the subject it needs to be), it is also extremely clear. The conclusions drawn from her long experience with psychotic children are shared with the diagnostician and practising therapist in helpful and non-esoteric language. In describing a particular feature of childhood psychosis, she is as careful to say what it is not as to say what it is, or seems to be, or is like. She also takes trouble to ground her theory in observations and detailed clinical case studies. My major reservation about the book concerns a place where the speculation seems to outstrip observation, but I will return to this point later.
